title: Wake-up and extended-window thrombolysis
summary: Unknown onset within 4.5 h of symptom recognition with DWI–FLAIR mismatch: IVT can be beneficial (AHA 2026, 2a; WAKE-UP: mRS 0–1 53.3 vs 41.8%). Perfusion mismatch at 4.5–9 h, or within 9 h of the sleep midpoint, without EVT: IVT is reasonable (2a; EXTEND: 35.4 vs 29.5%, sICH 6.2 vs 0.9%). LVO at 4.5–24 h with salvageable tissue and no EVT access: IVT may be beneficial (2b; TRACE-III tenecteplase 33.0 vs 24.2%, sICH 3.0 vs 0.8%). With EVT planned, late tenecteplase added nothing (TIMELESS; TNK-PLUS).

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with unknown onset time who are within 4.5 hours of symptom recognition and have a DWI lesion smaller than one-third of MCA territory with no marked FLAIR signal change, IVT within 4.5 hours of symptom recognition can be beneficial to improve functional outcomes.

For AIS patients ineligible for EVT who have salvageable penumbra on automated perfusion imaging, IVT can be beneficial within 4.5–9 hours of last known well or within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep for wake-up stroke.

In AIS patients with LVO and salvageable ischemic penumbra, presenting 4.5-24 hours from symptom onset or last known well, who cannot receive EVT, IVT directed by clinicians with expertise in thrombolytic stroke care may be beneficial to improve functional outcomes.

consider: Perfusion mismatch at 4.5–24 h without planned EVT (China): OPTION (non-LVO, tenecteplase; mRS 0–1 43.6 vs 34.2%, sICH 2.8 vs 0%) and HOPE (with or without LVO, alteplase; 40 vs 26%, sICH 3.8 vs 0.5%) were positive.
Posterior circulation at 4.5–24 h, mostly mild, no EVT: EXPECTS (alteplase) functional independence 89.6 vs 72.6%.
Pin down last known well, symptom discovery and the imaging route (MRI mismatch vs automated perfusion).
caution: Late-window benefit comes from imaging-selected, mostly Chinese cohorts and costs more sICH.

title: Minor stroke, TIA and short-course antiplatelets
summary: Noncardioembolic minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4) within 24 h without IVT: aspirin plus clopidogrel with a loading dose for 21 days, then one agent (AHA 2026, COR 1). CHANCE: stroke 8.2 vs 11.7%; POINT: major ischemic events 5.0 vs 6.5% with major hemorrhage 0.9 vs 0.4%. Alternatives: ticagrelor plus aspirin for 30 days (NIHSS ≤5; THALES 5.5 vs 6.6%, severe bleeding 0.5 vs 0.1%); presumed atherosclerotic at 24–72 h: clopidogrel plus aspirin for 21 days (INSPIRES 7.3 vs 9.2%); CYP2C19 loss-of-function: ticagrelor plus aspirin (CHANCE-2 6.0 vs 7.6%).

recommendations.text: In patients with minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 3 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or greater) who did not receive IVT, DAPT (aspirin plus clopidogrel with loading dose) is recommended to be initiated within 24 hours of symptom onset and continued for 21 days, followed by single antiplatelet therapy, to reduce the 90-day risk of recurrent ischemic stroke.

In patients with recent (under 24 hours) minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 5 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 6 or greater, or symptomatic intracranial/extracranial stenosis 50% or greater) who did not receive IVT, DAPT with ticagrelor (including loading dose) plus aspirin for 30 days may be considered to reduce 30-day recurrent stroke risk.

In patients with minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 5 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or greater) within 24-72 hours of onset (or NIHSS 4-5 within 24 hours) who did not receive IVT and have presumed atherosclerotic cause (50% or greater intracranial or extracranial stenosis or acute infarctions of presumed large artery origin), DAPT (clopidogrel plus aspirin) for 21 days followed by SAPT is reasonable to reduce 90-day recurrent stroke risk.

consider: Disabling deficit? Assess for IVT/EVT first. Non-disabling: DAPT was noninferior to alteplase (ARAMIS), and alteplase gave no benefit (PRISMS).
Write the stop date (day 21 or 30) and the single agent to continue.
After IVT (NIHSS 4–10), TAPIS started aspirin plus ticagrelor within 6 h with better mRS 0–1 (68.7 vs 62.0%); AHA 2026 still rates antiplatelets in the first 24 h after IVT as uncertain.
caution: Do not extend DAPT beyond 21–30 days without a separate indication; bleeding rose with DAPT in POINT, THALES and INSPIRES.

title: Thrombolytic agent and evidence selection
summary: Within 4.5 h use tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) as a single bolus or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) (AHA 2026, COR 1); tenecteplase is preferred before EVT for LVO (ESO 2023, strong). Tenecteplase was noninferior in AcT, ATTEST-2 (OR 1.07), TRACE-2 and ORIGINAL, and doubled early reperfusion before EVT in EXTEND-IA TNK (22 vs 10%). Do not use tenecteplase 0.4 mg/kg (COR 3). Reteplase or mutant prourokinase may be considered when EVT is not planned (2b).

recommendations.text: In adult AIS patients presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset or last known well who are eligible for IVT, tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) is recommended to improve functional outcomes.
In adult AIS patients presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset or last known well who are eligible for IVT, tenecteplase at a dose of 0.4 mg/kg is not recommended.

consider: Use the agent and dose source your protocol specifies, and dose from the patient's weight with the calculator.
Angioedema occurred in 1% with either agent (ATTEST-2): be ready to manage the airway and bleeding.
Not recommended: desmoteplase, urokinase, streptokinase and sonothrombolysis (COR 3).
caution: A positive trial does not establish local approval or availability of a newer thrombolytic.

title: Thrombectomy selection and bridging thrombolysis
summary: Anterior LVO (ICA or M1), NIHSS ≥6, prestroke mRS 0–1: EVT within 6 h if ASPECTS 3–10, and at 6–24 h if ASPECTS ≥6 (AHA 2026, COR 1). HERMES (≤6 h): mRS shift cOR 2.49; DAWN (6–24 h, clinical–core mismatch): mRS 0–2 49 vs 13%; DEFUSE 3 (6–16 h, perfusion mismatch): 45 vs 17%. Give IVT first when eligible and do not delay EVT: EVT alone was not shown noninferior in SWIFT DIRECT or MR CLEAN-NO IV, and BRIDGE-TNK favored tenecteplase first (mRS 0–2 52.9 vs 44.1%).

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1), presenting within 6 hours of symptom onset, with NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, and ASPECTS 3-10, EVT (endovascular thrombectomy) is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting 6-24 hours from symptom onset, with NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, and ASPECTS 6 or greater, EVT is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting within 6 hours, NIHSS 6 or greater, ASPECTS 6 or greater, and prestroke mRS of 2, EVT is reasonable to improve functional outcomes and reduce accumulated disability.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting within 6 hours, NIHSS 6 or greater, ASPECTS 6 or greater, and prestroke mRS of 3-4, EVT might be reasonable to improve functional outcomes and reduce accumulated disability.

consider: Prestroke mRS 2: EVT is reasonable (2a); mRS 3–4 within 6 h: EVT might be reasonable (2b).
Transfers: go straight to angiography without repeat imaging unless the exam changed or the transfer was delayed (2b).
Large core, basilar, MeVO and perfusion details: see the dedicated cards.
caution: DIRECT-MT (China) found EVT alone noninferior, but European trials did not; give IVT whenever eligible.

title: Large-core infarction and thrombectomy
summary: Large cores still benefit: ASPECTS 3–5 at 6–24 h (age <80, mRS 0–1, no significant mass effect) is COR 1, and ASPECTS 0–2 within 6 h is reasonable (2a) (AHA 2026). SELECT2: generalized OR 1.51 (mRS 0–2 20 vs 7%); ANGEL-ASPECT: GOR 1.37; RESCUE-Japan LIMIT: mRS 0–3 31.0 vs 12.7%; TENSION: cOR 2.58 with lower mortality; LASTE (ASPECTS ≤5 within 6.5 h): mortality 36.1 vs 55.5%. Expect more hemorrhage (ANGEL-ASPECT sICH 6.1 vs 2.7%).

recommendations.text: In selected patients with AIS from anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1), presenting 6-24 hours from symptom onset, age under 80, NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, ASPECTS 3-5, and without significant mass effect on imaging, EVT is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

In selected AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting within 6 hours, age under 80, NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, ASPECTS 0-2, and without significant mass effect, EVT is reasonable to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

consider: Measure the core consistently (NCCT/MRI ASPECTS or CTP core) and confirm age, baseline mRS and mass effect.
Set expectations: the benefit is mostly less disability, not independence (LASTE median mRS 4 vs 6).
SVIN 2025: ASPECTS 0–2 at 6–24 h — benefit uncertain (2b).
caution: Trials mostly enrolled patients aged 80 or younger with prestroke mRS 0–1.

title: Basilar artery occlusion
summary: Basilar occlusion with NIHSS ≥10, PC-ASPECTS ≥6 and baseline mRS 0–1: EVT within 24 h (AHA 2026, COR 1). ATTENTION (≤12 h): mRS 0–3 46 vs 23%, mortality 37 vs 55%; BAOCHE (6–24 h): 46 vs 24%. NIHSS 6–9: benefit not established (2b; ESO suggests best medical treatment for NIHSS <10). Give IVT if eligible (ESO suggests IVT plus EVT over direct EVT); TRACE-5 tenecteplase within 24 h improved mRS 0–1 or return to baseline (38 vs 29%), but ATTENTION LATE found no gain from tenecteplase before EVT at 4.5–24 h (30 vs 30%).

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with basilar artery occlusion, baseline mRS 0-1, NIHSS 10 or greater, and PC-ASPECTS 6 or greater (mild ischemic damage), EVT within 24 hours of symptom onset is recommended to achieve better functional outcome and reduce mortality.

In AIS patients with basilar artery occlusion, baseline mRS 0-1, NIHSS 6-9, and PC-ASPECTS 6 or greater, the effectiveness of EVT within 24 hours for improving functional outcomes and reducing mortality is not well established.

consider: A low NIHSS can understate posterior-circulation disability; recheck for fluctuation.
Very extensive bilateral or brainstem infarction: ESO consensus suggests no reperfusion; with PC-ASPECTS 0–6, weigh age, frailty and prestroke disability.
First pass: aspiration is suggested over a stent retriever (ESO, weak); rescue angioplasty or stenting for an underlying stenosis after failed EVT (consensus).
caution: Most trial patients were Chinese with severe deficits; evidence for mild BAO is weak.

title: Medium and distal vessel occlusion
summary: Routine EVT for medium or distal occlusion is not supported: DISTAL (n=543), ESCAPE-MeVO (n=530) and DISCOUNT (n=244, stopped for futility and excess sICH) showed no functional benefit, with more sICH (DISCOUNT 11 vs 3% among those treated) and higher mortality in ESCAPE-MeVO (13.3 vs 8.4%). ORIENTAL-MeVO (China, NIHSS ≥6, ≤24 h) is the only positive trial (mRS 0–2 58.6 vs 46.6%; sICH 4.7 vs 2.2%). EVT remains reasonable for a disabling dominant or proximal M2 occlusion (AHA 2026, 2a; SVIN 2026, 2a).

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with occlusion of the dominant proximal M2 division of the MCA presenting within 6 hours, prestroke mRS 0-1, NIHSS 6 or greater, and ASPECTS 6 or greater, EVT is reasonable to improve functional outcomes, though benefits are uncertain.

In AIS patients with occlusion of the proximal nondominant or codominant M2 segment, distal MCA, anterior cerebral artery, or posterior cerebral artery, EVT is not recommended as it does not improve functional outcomes.

EVT is reasonable for patients with disabling stroke due to proximal and/or dominant M2 occlusions, particularly when associated with moderate-to-severe deficits and imaging evidence of salvageable brain tissue.

consider: Confirm the segment (dominant vs codominant/nondominant M2, M3, ACA, PCA), a disabling deficit and IVT eligibility; give IVT if eligible.
SVIN 2026: EVT may be considered case by case for disabling ACA or PCA occlusion; it is not standard for M3/M4.
Review ORIENTAL-MeVO's population limits with the intervention team.
caution: The AHA 2026 grading predates ORIENTAL-MeVO and DISCOUNT; one positive Chinese trial does not establish benefit for every M2 or distal lesion.

title: Acute retinal ischemia and CRAO
summary: Treat acute central retinal artery occlusion as an ischemic stroke and an emergency: same-day stroke workup and vascular risk-factor treatment, urgent ophthalmology, and assessment for an arteritic cause. IVT within 4.5 h has uncertain usefulness (AHA 2026, 2b): THEIA (alteplase vs aspirin) and TenCRAOS (tenecteplase) showed no significant visual benefit, and TenCRAOS had one fatal intracranial hemorrhage.
consider: Confirm the ophthalmic diagnosis and onset; coordinate stroke and ophthalmology assessment.
Both trials studied nonarteritic CRAO; suspected arteritis needs its own pathway.
THEIA measured visual acuity and TenCRAOS a vision-recovery threshold; weigh safety alongside benefit.
caution: Small neutral trials do not prove equivalence, and the 2021 AHA statement predates them.

title: EVT technique, anesthesia and rescue questions
summary: Aim for eTICI 2b–3 as early as possible with a stent retriever, aspiration or both (AHA 2026, COR 1); general anesthesia or procedural sedation are both acceptable (COR 1). Tandem lesions: treating both may be reasonable (2b). Intra-arterial thrombolytic after mTICI ≥2b may be reasonable (2b); preprocedural tirofiban is not useful (COR 3). Rescue angioplasty or stenting after failed EVT remains uncertain (2b).
consider: Document final eTICI, complications, access site and the BP plan for the receiving team.
Tandem stenting or rescue stenting commits the patient to antiplatelets — weigh hemorrhage risk.
Avoid SBP drops during the procedure (ESO 2026).
caution: Technique choices depend on operator expertise and devices; this card is not a procedural protocol.

title: Malignant infarction: hemicraniectomy and cerebellar decompression
summary: Age ≤60 with unilateral MCA infarction deteriorating within 48 h despite medical therapy: decompressive craniectomy (AHA 2026, COR 1) — pooled DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET: survival 78 vs 29% and mRS ≤3 43 vs 21% (NNT 2 and 4). Over 60: may be considered to reduce mortality (2b); DESTINY II (61–82 y) doubled survival with mRS 0–4 (38 vs 18%), but no one reached mRS 0–2. Cerebellar infarction: ventriculostomy for obstructive hydrocephalus; suboccipital decompression for brainstem compression or volume ≥35 mL (COR 1).

recommendations.text: In patients 60 years of age or younger with unilateral MCA infarctions who deteriorate neurologically within 48 hours from brain swelling despite medical therapy, decompressive craniectomy with dural expansion is recommended to reduce mortality and improve functional outcome.

In patients over 60 years of age with unilateral MCA infarctions who deteriorate neurologically within 48 hours from brain swelling despite medical therapy, decompressive craniectomy with dural expansion may be considered to reduce mortality.

In patients with cerebellar infarction and obstructive hydrocephalus, ventriculostomy is recommended to improve neurological function and decrease mortality. Concomitant or subsequent decompressive craniectomy may or may not be necessary based on infarction size, neurological condition, degree of brainstem compression, and effectiveness of medical management.

In patients with cerebellar infarction causing neurological deterioration from brainstem compression or infarct volumes 35 mL or greater, decompressive suboccipital craniectomy with dural expansion is recommended to improve outcomes and decrease mortality.

consider: Discuss goals early and transfer large MCA or cerebellar infarcts to a neurosurgical center before they swell.
Falling consciousness from swelling is a reasonable trigger for surgery (2a); use osmotherapy only as a bridge.
Avoid hypothermia, barbiturates and corticosteroids for swelling; IV glibenclamide did not help (COR 3).
caution: Surgery saves lives, but most older survivors need help with daily care; decide with the outcomes the patient would accept.

title: Acute blood pressure targets by pathway
summary: Before IVT <185/110; after IVT <180/105 for at least 24 h; during and for 24 h after EVT ≤180/105 (AHA 2026; ESO 2026). After successful EVT do not target SBP <140 (AHA 2026, harm): ENCHANTED2/MT (<120) worsened mRS (OR 1.37) and OPTIMAL-BP (<140) lowered mRS 0–2 from 54.4 to 39.4%. One Spanish trial (HOPE) found reperfusion-guided targets (140–160 for mTICI 2b; 100–140 for 2c/3) improved mRS 0–2 (60.0 vs 47.1%). No reperfusion and <220/120: starting treatment in the first 48–72 h does not help; ≥220/120: benefit uncertain (ESO: lower by <15% over 24 h). No routine prehospital lowering (INTERACT4: ischemic stroke cOR 1.30).

recommendations.text: AIS patients with elevated BP who are otherwise eligible for IVT are recommended to have SBP lowered below 185 mmHg and DBP below 110 mmHg before initiating IVT therapy to reduce hemorrhagic complications.
After IVT treatment, BP is recommended to be maintained below 180/105 mmHg for at least the first 24 hours.
In patients who undergo EVT, it is reasonable to maintain BP at or below 180/105 mmHg during and for 24 hours after the procedure.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation LVO who have been successfully recanalized by EVT (mTICI 2b, 2c, or 3) without other indications for specific BP targets, intensive SBP reduction to below 140 mmHg for the first 72 hours is harmful and not recommended.

In patients with mild to moderate severity AIS treated with IVT, intensive SBP reduction (target below 140 mmHg compared with below 180 mmHg) is not recommended as it does not improve functional outcome.

consider: After alteplase, SBP 130–140 did not improve outcome versus <180 (ENCHANTED; AHA 2026 COR 3).
Treat hypertension early only when a comorbidity demands it (ACS, heart failure, aortic dissection, post-IVT sICH, preeclampsia); correct hypotension and hypovolemia.
Hold home oral antihypertensives while swallowing is unsafe; ESO advises against routinely continuing them in the acute phase.
caution: One number does not fit every pathway; ICH and long-term targets are on their own cards.

title: Antithrombotic-associated ICH: reversal
summary: Stop the drug and reverse as soon as ICH is diagnosed (AHA 2022, COR 1). Factor Xa inhibitor: 4F-PCC rather than andexanet (NCS/SCCM 2026, conditional); andexanet (Andexxa) was withdrawn from the US market effective 22 December 2025. Warfarin with INR ≥2.0: 4F-PCC over FFP, then IV vitamin K (COR 1). Dabigatran: idarucizumab (2a). Heparin: protamine (2a). Antiplatelets: no platelet transfusion unless neurosurgery is planned; if on aspirin and going to surgery, transfuse platelets (conditional). No recommendation on desmopressin or on reversal in small ICH.

recommendations.text: Immediate discontinuation of anticoagulation and rapid reversal are recommended as soon as possible after diagnosis of anticoagulant-associated spontaneous ICH to improve survival.
We suggest using 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate rather than andexanet alfa in patients with factor Xa inhibitor-associated spontaneous ICH.
We suggest against administering platelet transfusions to patients with spontaneous intraparenchymal hemorrhage taking antiplatelet agents who do not require neurosurgical intervention.
We suggest administering platelet transfusions to patients with spontaneous intraparenchymal hemorrhage who were on aspirin therapy who require neurosurgical intervention.
4-factor PCC is recommended over FFP for patients with VKA-associated spontaneous ICH and INR ≥ 2.0 to achieve rapid INR correction and limit hemorrhage expansion.
Idarucizumab is reasonable for patients with dabigatran-associated spontaneous ICH to reverse the anticoagulant effect.

consider: Record drug, dose, last intake and renal function; activated charcoal may help if a DOAC was taken within the previous few hours (2b).
Dabigatran without idarucizumab: PCC/aPCC or renal replacement therapy may be considered (2b).
Traumatic ICH: viscoelastic-assay-guided treatment if available (NCS/SCCM 2026).
caution: ANNEXA-I's better hemostasis came with more thrombotic events and no functional gain; take doses from the ICH protocol.

title: CAA, lobar hemorrhage and recurrence risk
summary: Suspect CAA with lobar ICH, convexity SAH or transient focal episodes; MRI with blood-sensitive sequences looks for lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis. Recurrence risk rises with lobar location, older age, more lobar microbleeds, disseminated superficial siderosis, poor BP control and APOE ε2/ε4 (AHA 2022, 2a). Restarting antiplatelets may be reasonable (2b; RESTART: recurrent ICH 4 vs 9%, not significant). In AF after ICH, PRESTIGE-AF found fewer ischemic strokes but more recurrent ICH with DOACs — individualize; left atrial appendage closure may be considered if anticoagulation is not possible (2b).
consider: Transient focal episodes may be CAA rather than TIA — avoid reflex antithrombotics.
Long-term BP <130/80 is reasonable after ICH (AHA 2022, 2a).
Ask about antiamyloid therapy; CAA changes those decisions.
caution: Recurrence estimates are population averages, not an individual prognosis.

title: Unruptured intracranial aneurysm review
summary: Weigh rupture risk (size, location, growth, morphology, prior SAH; PHASES, ELAPSS and UIATS support the discussion) against treatment risk and patient preference in a multidisciplinary team. Stop smoking and treat hypertension. Most ESO recommendations rest on very low-certainty evidence.
consider: Review aneurysm size, location, morphology, growth and prior hemorrhage alongside patient factors.
Clarify the purpose and interval of surveillance with the treating team.
Discuss treatment alternatives, smoking/BP review and preferences in a multidisciplinary setting.
caution: Scores support discussion; they do not choose a procedure or capture every relevant feature.

title: Seizures after stroke: treatment versus prophylaxis
summary: Treat clinical or EEG-confirmed seizures. Do not give prophylactic antiseizure drugs after ischemic stroke or ICH without seizures (AHA 2026; AHA 2022: no benefit). After aSAH, brief prophylaxis may be reasonable only with high-risk features; avoid phenytoin. Use continuous EEG (at least 24 h) for unexplained or fluctuating mental status after ICH.

recommendations.text: In adult AIS patients, prophylactic antiseizure medication is not recommended as it does not prevent seizures or improve functional outcome.
Prophylactic antiseizure medication is not beneficial for patients with spontaneous ICH who have no evidence of seizures with regard to functional outcomes, long-term seizure control, or mortality.

consider: After an unprovoked poststroke seizure, choose the antiseizure drug by patient factors (AHA 2026, COR 1).
Document the indication and a review date for any antiseizure drug continued at discharge.
aSAH with a seizure at onset: treat for no more than 7 days; longer courses do not reduce later seizures.
caution: Permissive prophylaxis recommendations do not justify indefinite treatment.

title: Functional seizures and diagnostic communication
summary: Make a positive diagnosis from the event history, witness accounts and, when feasible, video-EEG of a typical event; explain it respectfully, screen for coexisting epilepsy and psychiatric conditions, and arrange continuity (AAN 2025). Reassess antiseizure or benzodiazepine exposure against any coexisting indication.
consider: Review event history, witness information and typical-event recording or video-EEG when feasible.
Explain the diagnostic rationale and arrange continuity rather than relying on a label alone.
Reassess ASM or benzodiazepine exposure against any coexisting indication.
caution: Functional seizures and epilepsy can coexist; a normal routine EEG or one bedside sign does not make the diagnosis.

title: Stroke prognosis: timing, confounders and uncertainty
summary: Do not settle prognosis on day 1. After ICH, full care with new DNAR or withdrawal deferred until at least the second full hospital day is reasonable unless prior wishes say otherwise (AHA 2022, 2a). Severity scores such as the ICH score frame discussion but must not be the sole basis to limit treatment (COR 3), and a DNAR order alone should not limit other care. Clear confounders such as sedation and medical instability first (NCS).

recommendations.text: A baseline severity score alone is not recommended as the sole basis for forecasting individual prognosis or deciding to limit life-sustaining treatment in patients with spontaneous ICH.

consider: Identify sedation, medical instability and other confounders before discussing prognosis.
Explain the outcome being estimated, the time horizon and the range of uncertainty.
Revisit recovery over time and incorporate what outcomes the patient would value.
caution: Premature withdrawal can distort both individual care and the evidence used to estimate prognosis.

title: Consent, goals of care and palliative support
summary: Offer palliative support alongside restorative stroke care. With large cerebral or cerebellar infarcts at risk of swelling, discuss options and likely outcomes early (AHA 2026, COR 1). Clarify capacity and the appropriate surrogate, and use shared decision-making for patients who cannot fully participate (AHA 2022, 2a).
consider: Clarify capacity, the appropriate surrogate and known preferences.
Explain the decision, alternatives and uncertainty in language suited to the situation.
Identify symptom burden, psychosocial needs and when specialist support would help.
caution: Palliative care is not withdrawal of treatment; emergency consent rules depend on the setting.

title: BD/DNC: determination and communication resources
summary: Use the institutional BD/DNC process and the 2023 multisociety guideline for prerequisites, confounders, examination, apnea testing and ancillary-test indications; the 2025 AAN statement covers communication, objections, pregnancy and public trust.
consider: Use the complete institutional process for prerequisites, confounders and examiner qualifications.
Consult the guideline for neurologic examination, apnea testing and valid ancillary-test indications.
Plan clear communication and address accommodations or objections through the relevant process.

title: Moyamoya disease and syndrome
summary: Moyamoya with ischemic stroke or TIA: direct or indirect extracranial–intracranial bypass can prevent recurrent ischemia (AHA 2021, 2a); refer to an experienced center. Distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic presentations and moyamoya disease from secondary moyamoya syndrome, and review perfusion studies and the antithrombotic rationale.
consider: Confirm the vascular pattern and whether a secondary moyamoya syndrome is plausible.
Review recurrent symptoms, perfusion studies and hemorrhagic features with an experienced team.
Clarify surveillance, perioperative planning and the rationale for any antithrombotic therapy.
caution: Do not manage moyamoya as ordinary atherosclerotic stenosis.

title: Suspected primary CNS vasculitis
summary: Do not diagnose PACNS from imaging alone: no single MRI pattern or routine CSF abnormality establishes it. Exclude RCVS, infection and other mimics, and confirm with expert multidisciplinary review, including tissue diagnosis when needed, before prolonged immunotherapy (ESO 2023).
consider: Review alternative vascular, infectious, inflammatory and noninflammatory explanations.
Discuss the roles and limitations of vascular imaging, CSF studies and tissue diagnosis.
Clarify what evidence supports the diagnosis before committing to prolonged immunotherapy.
caution: Evidence is sparse, and vessel imaging alone cannot separate PACNS from mimics such as RCVS.

title: RCVS and PRES
summary: Recurrent thunderclap headaches with segmental cerebral vasoconstriction suggest RCVS; over half of cases are postpartum or follow adrenergic or serotonergic drugs. Vasoconstriction peaks 2–3 weeks after onset and resolves within 3 months, and stroke can follow initially normal imaging. RCVS2 (thunderclap headache, carotid involvement, vasoconstrictive trigger, sex, SAH; range −2 to +10): ≥5 was 99% specific and 90% sensitive for RCVS; ≤2 was 100% specific for excluding it, including against PACNS. PRES (bilateral subcortical vasogenic edema) follows BP fluctuation, renal failure, cytotoxic drugs, autoimmune disease or eclampsia, and usually resolves.
consider: Exclude aneurysmal SAH first and remove vasoactive triggers.
Repeat vessel imaging if early imaging is normal but suspicion persists.
Nimodipine may ease thunderclap headache within 48 h but has no proven effect on stroke or hemorrhage.
PRES: treat the driver (BP, drug, eclampsia) and watch for hemorrhage or posterior-fossa edema with hydrocephalus.
caution: Evidence is observational; RCVS2 was derived from 30 RCVS patients at one center.

title: Spinal cord infarction
summary: Suspect spinal cord infarction with sudden severe myelopathy reaching its nadir within 12 h (77% of 133 Mayo patients; 76% had vascular risk factors). The first spine MRI was normal in 24%, so repeat it with DWI and axial T2: owl-eye (65%) or pencil-like (40%) T2 signal, and DWI restriction in 67% of those imaged. Supportive findings: adjacent arterial dissection or occlusion (20%) and vertebral body infarction (9%); CSF was inflammatory in only 8%.
consider: Recent aortic surgery or repair, hypotension or vertebral dissection?
Selective pain and temperature loss (39%) and a stuttering course (23%) occur; do not label transverse myelitis too early.
Apply the proposed definite, probable and possible criteria, and exclude cord compression.
caution: The criteria come from one center, and acute treatments lack randomized evidence.

title: Inherited small-vessel disease and CADASIL
summary: Suspect CADASIL or another inherited small-vessel disease when age, family history, clinical pattern and MRI phenotype fit; confirm molecularly with genetic counseling, and treat vascular risk factors while separating established care from unproven disease-modifying treatment (AHA 2023).
consider: Review the age, family history, clinical pattern and imaging phenotype together.
Consider genetic counseling and the implications of testing for the patient and relatives.
Address modifiable vascular factors while distinguishing established care from unproven disease-modifying treatment.
caution: A suggestive MRI pattern is not a molecular diagnosis.

title: Lacunar stroke and covert small-vessel disease
summary: Lacunar stroke and covert small-vessel disease are different populations (ESO). Symptomatic lacunar stroke gets standard secondary prevention with antiplatelet, BP and lipid treatment; in SPS3, SBP <130 vs 130–149 did not significantly reduce all stroke but reduced ICH (HR 0.37). Address cognition and gait when relevant.
consider: Is there a corresponding clinical stroke syndrome or only an incidental imaging finding?
Review BP, lifestyle and competing stroke mechanisms rather than assuming every small lesion is lacunar.
Address cognition, gait and functional consequences when clinically relevant.
caution: Do not start an antiplatelet solely for incidental white-matter changes.

title: LV thrombus, LV dysfunction and other cardiac sources
summary: LV thrombus with stroke: warfarin for at least 3 months (AHA 2021, COR 1); DOAC safety for a new LV thrombus is uncertain (2b). Reduced ejection fraction without thrombus is not by itself an anticoagulation indication. Mechanical valves: warfarin — dabigatran (RE-ALIGN) and apixaban (PROACT Xa) caused more thromboembolism. Mechanical assist device: warfarin plus aspirin can be beneficial (2a).
consider: Clarify the suspected source and whether the cardiac imaging adequately addresses it.
Review valve/device status, rhythm, ventricular function and the antithrombotic indication with cardiology.
Consider bleeding risk and concurrent antiplatelet exposure when discussing therapy.
caution: Prosthetic valves and circulatory support devices need their own specialist pathways.

title: Stroke with suspected infective endocarditis
summary: Suspected endocarditis with stroke: involve cardiology, infectious diseases and cardiac surgery early. Recurrent emboli with persistent vegetations despite antibiotics: early surgery is reasonable if there is no ICH or extensive brain injury (AHA 2021, 2a); with a major stroke or ICH, delaying valve surgery for at least 4 weeks may be considered (2b).
consider: Assess whether the presentation warrants an endocarditis evaluation and multidisciplinary team involvement.
Clarify the neurologic complication and any hemorrhage or infective aneurysm concern.
Coordinate antimicrobial, valve/device and surgical timing decisions with neurology, cardiology and infectious diseases.
caution: Do not apply a routine cardioembolic-stroke pathway without checking the endocarditis-specific guidance.

title: First-stroke prevention and metabolic health
summary: Prevention without prior stroke: control BP, lipids and glucose, stop tobacco, and address activity, diet, weight and sleep (AHA/ASA 2024), including sex-specific risk factors.
consider: Review BP, lipids, glycemia, tobacco exposure, activity, diet, weight and sleep in context.
Clarify sex-specific and other risk factors that affect the prevention discussion.
Assess medication indications, access and adherence using the relevant disease-specific guidance.
caution: Evidence for a metabolic drug in one population does not establish an indication in every stroke-risk group.

title: AF stroke prevention beyond start timing
summary: After stroke or TIA with AF, anticoagulate regardless of AF pattern; use a DOAC over warfarin unless there is moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve (AHA 2021, COR 1). Do not routinely add an antiplatelet without active coronary disease or a recent stent (AHA 2026, harm). Device-detected subclinical AF: apixaban reduced stroke and embolism but increased major bleeding (ARTESiA), while edoxaban did not help (NOAH-AFNET 6). Cannot take long-term anticoagulation: left atrial appendage closure may be reasonable (2b). Rheumatic AF: rivaroxaban was worse than a VKA (INVICTUS).
consider: Confirm how AF was documented, its clinical context and the actual thromboembolic indication.
Review valve disease, renal function, interactions, prior bleeding and concurrent antiplatelets.
If considering LAAO or a device-detected AF strategy, review that specific evidence and follow-up requirements.
caution: Valve- and device-specific evidence overrides general AF risk scores.

title: Lipids, vascular risk and treatment follow-up
summary: Atherosclerotic stroke or TIA: statin ± ezetimibe to LDL <70 mg/dL (AHA 2021, COR 1; Treat Stroke to Target events 8.5 vs 10.9%). No known coronary disease and LDL >100: atorvastatin 80 mg (COR 1; SPARCL stroke 11.2 vs 13.1%, with more hemorrhagic strokes). Very high risk above 70 on statin plus ezetimibe: add a PCSK9 inhibitor (2a). Recheck lipids 4–12 weeks after starting or changing therapy.
consider: Clarify the vascular indication, lipid profile, prior treatment and adherence.
Triglycerides 135–499 mg/dL on a statin: icosapent ethyl is reasonable in selected patients (2a).
After ICH, weigh statin benefit against hemorrhage risk individually (AHA 2022, 2b).
caution: The 2026 dyslipidemia guideline sets risk-specific goals; check it for thresholds beyond this card.

title: Long-term blood pressure prevention
summary: After stroke or TIA, target office BP <130/80 for most (AHA 2021, COR 1), and treat if ≥130/80 even without prior hypertension (2a). PROGRESS: perindopril plus indapamide lowered BP by 12/5 mm Hg and stroke by 43%, whereas perindopril alone (5/3 mm Hg) gave no clear reduction. After ICH, long-term SBP <130 and DBP <80 is reasonable (AHA 2022, 2a); the TRIDENT low-dose triple pill reduced recurrent stroke (4.6 vs 7.4%; HR 0.61). Lacunar stroke: SPS3 (<130) reduced ICH.
consider: Confirm measurement technique, home readings and possible orthostatic symptoms.
Review adherence, reversible contributors and access to treatment.
Individualize the follow-up and medication plan using current guidance and comorbidities.
caution: Long-term targets do not apply in the acute phase.

title: Brain arteriovenous malformation
summary: Separate ruptured from unruptured AVMs and decide with a multidisciplinary vascular team, weighing natural history against surgical, endovascular and radiosurgical risks (AHA/ASA 2017).
consider: Clarify rupture status, anatomy, symptoms and associated lesions.
Review expected natural history and treatment risks with a multidisciplinary vascular team.
Discuss the specific treatment goal and follow-up plan with the patient.
caution: The 2017 statement is dated, and no grading scale or single trial selects treatment for every AVM.

title: Cerebral and spinal cavernous malformation
summary: Establish lesion location, prior symptomatic hemorrhage, seizures and whether lesions are familial or multiple, then plan imaging, genetic counseling and any intervention in a specialist setting; evidence gaps remain substantial (2025 consensus).
consider: Clarify lesion location, prior symptomatic hemorrhage, seizures and whether lesions are familial or multiple.
Review imaging, genetic counseling and follow-up needs in the appropriate specialty setting.
Compare intervention risks with the clinical history and the outcomes the patient values.
caution: Many recommendations rely on limited evidence, and incidental and symptomatic brainstem or spinal lesions need different discussions.

title: aSAH critical care and CSF diversion
summary: Keep euvolemia (AHA 2023, 2a); induced hypervolemia and prophylactic hemodynamic augmentation are harmful (COR 3). Monitor for DCI with frequent exams, TCD, and CTA or CT perfusion when the exam is unreliable (2a). Symptomatic vasospasm: raising SBP, intra-arterial vasodilators or angioplasty may be reasonable (2b). Acute symptomatic hydrocephalus: EVD and/or lumbar drainage (COR 1) under a bundled EVD protocol. EARLYDRAIN (lumbar drain after securing) reduced poor outcome, but ESO 2026 makes no recommendation on prophylactic lumbar drainage.
consider: Do not drain CSF for radiological hydrocephalus alone when consciousness is normal (ESO consensus).
Liberal transfusion (Hb ≤10 g/dL) did not improve 12-month outcome (SAHaRA).
Start VTE prophylaxis once the aneurysm is secured (COR 1).
caution: Drain management needs the full neurosurgical protocol.

title: New and adjunct therapies: match the evidence
summary: Asundexian (factor XIa inhibitor) added to antiplatelets reduced ischemic stroke after noncardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA (OCEANIC-STROKE 6.2 vs 8.4%; major bleeding 1.9 vs 1.7%) but was worse than apixaban in AF (OCEANIC-AF). Adjunctive IV argatroban or eptifibatide after IVT did not help and increased mortality (MOST: 24% and 12% vs 8%). Nerinetide (ESCAPE-NEXT), prehospital remote ischemic conditioning (RESIST) and colchicine (CONVINCE, CHANCE-3) were neutral; SERIC-EVT (conditioning after EVT) is a single positive trial.
consider: Compare the population, background therapy and primary endpoint with your patient before applying a new result.
Separate confirmatory results from subgroup signals, and look for independent replication.
Confirm regulatory approval and local availability before using any new agent.
caution: Neuroprotective agents and IV argatroban are not recommended outside trials (AHA 2026, COR 3).

title: Rapid appraisal of a trial or guideline
summary: Use a structured appraisal before converting a study headline into a clinical decision: population, comparison, outcome, uncertainty and applicability.
consider: Is the outcome patient-important, and is the quoted result the prespecified primary analysis?
Compare absolute and relative effects, confidence intervals, missing data and harms.
Check whether subgroup, noninferiority or composite-endpoint claims support the proposed inference.
caution: A neutral superiority trial does not prove equivalence.

title: ICH expansion and intraventricular extension
summary: No hemostatic drug improves function: recombinant factor VIIa within 2 h (FASTEST) slowed growth by 3.7 mL but did not change 180-day mRS (cOR 1.09) and increased life-threatening thromboembolism (RR 3.41); tranexamic acid (TICH-2) also gave no functional benefit (aOR 0.88). IVH with hydrocephalus and reduced consciousness: EVD (AHA 2022, COR 1). Intraventricular alteplase through an EVD lowered 180-day mortality (18 vs 29%) without improving mRS ≤3 and increased mRS 5 (CLEAR III).
consider: Is the problem expansion, ventricular obstruction, hydrocephalus or mass effect?
Repeat CT within 24 h, sooner with any decline, to catch expansion.
Discuss procedural risks and patient-valued outcomes with neurosurgery.
caution: Lower mortality without functional gain can mean more survivors with severe disability.

title: Antiphospholipid syndrome and stroke
summary: APS assessment connects the clinical thrombotic history with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies. An isolated positive test does not establish APS; acute illness and anticoagulants can distort lupus-anticoagulant testing.
consider: Does the stroke mechanism, age, vascular-risk profile or prior thrombotic/obstetric history justify targeted testing?
Review the antibody profile, assay conditions and repeat testing at least 12 weeks apart with hematology and the laboratory.
For established APS-associated stroke, review its specific antithrombotic evidence; DOAC results from AF should not be transferred to arterial APS.
caution: Classification criteria are not a standalone diagnostic test, and this card does not choose a drug, INR target or duration.

title: Sudden severe headache and suspected SAH
summary: Sudden severe headache warrants prompt evaluation for SAH and other serious causes. Interpret a negative CT with the onset interval, neurologic findings, scanner quality and reader expertise.
consider: Establish time to peak pain, onset time, examination findings and whether the presentation fits the source population.

AHA/ASA 2023 recommends LP after a negative CT when presentation is more than 6 hours after onset or there is a new neurologic deficit; early CT-only assessment has specific quality and examination requirements.
ACEP 2019 allows LP or CTA when SAH risk remains after negative CT, with shared discussion of limitations. Review these differing recommendations with the local diagnostic pathway.
caution: A negative CT is not universal clearance, and CTA can find an incidental aneurysm.

title: Fibromuscular dysplasia: vascular assessment and follow-up
summary: FMD is a nonatherosclerotic arterial disorder that can involve several vascular beds. The ESH/SVM consensus requires a focal or multifocal arterial lesion; dissection, aneurysm or tortuosity alone does not establish FMD.
consider: Review the vascular imaging diagnosis and any associated dissection, aneurysm or hypertension with an experienced team.
For established FMD, the 2019 consensus supports at least one brain-to-pelvis CTA or contrast-enhanced MRA assessment for additional disease, aneurysms and dissections.
Arrange longitudinal clinical review; customize subsequent imaging to the affected vessels, symptoms, prior procedures and aneurysm/dissection findings.
caution: Consensus guidance with limited treatment evidence; there is no universal follow-up imaging interval.
